cards.questionEn: How do you casually ask “what's up?” or ask what is happening?
cards.noteEn: The phrase can be a casual greeting or a genuine question about a situation. Qué keeps its written accent because it asks for information.

example.en: Hi, Marta. What's up?

cards.answerEn: the thing; what happened (as part of lo de)

cards.promptEs: lo de + tema, persona o momento
cards.questionEn: How do you refer informally to “the thing about” a topic or to what happened at a certain time?
cards.answerEn: Use lo de followed by the topic, person, or time reference.
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo leaves the event or matter unnamed, while de identifies it indirectly. The listener must recover the specific event or subject from context.

example.es: Tenemos que hablar de lo de ayer.
example.en: We have to talk about what happened yesterday.

cards.answerEn: about; from (as part of lo de)

cards.noteEn: Estuvo is a completed-past form of estar. With an evaluation such as bien or impresionante, it describes how an event or experience turned out.

example.en: The party was great.

cards.promptEs: el/la/los/las o un/una + adjetivo sin repetir el sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say “the interesting one” or “a small one” without repeating the noun?
cards.answerEn: Keep the article and adjective, omit the repeated noun, and make both agree with that understood noun.
cards.noteEn: The article is a word such as el, la, un, or una. The adjective still changes to match the omitted noun: una pequeña can mean “a small feminine one,” while uno pequeño can mean “a small masculine one.” Context supplies the missing noun.

example.es: Quiero una taza; dame la pequeña.
example.en: I want a cup; give me the small one.

cards.noteEn: With el, la, lo, los, or las, mejor usually means “best.” Without one of those words, it often means “better.”

example.en: This is the best option.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.answerEn: had (the completed-action form used after he)

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: I have to leave early.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

example.en: This is difficult.

cards.answerEn: is; is meant (in va en serio)
no separate English word; part of en serio (“seriously”)

cards.questionEn: How do you ask whether someone is really serious or whether something is actually true?
cards.answerEn: Use en serio to mean “seriously,” “really,” or “for real.”
cards.noteEn: En serio is a fixed expression. In a question, ¿En serio? often reacts with surprise or disbelief; in a statement, it can contrast sincerity with joking.

example.en: Are you really going to run tomorrow?

cards.noteEn: As a reaction, joder can express anger, shock, pain, or frustration. It is common in informal speech in Spain but is strongly vulgar and unsuitable for polite situations.

example.en: Fuck, I have lost the keys!

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; helps lo que mean “how much”
cards.noteEn: In an emphatic lo que followed by a verb, lo does not mean “it” or “the thing.” Together with que, it points to the amount or intensity of the action.

example.en: You have no idea how much it rained!

cards.questionEn: How can you emphasize how much an action happens or how strong its effect is?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que before the verb in an emphatic context, often after no sabes.
cards.noteEn: In this use, lo que works like English “how much,” not “what” or “the thing that.” A lead-in such as no sabes or an exclamatory tone selects the intensity reading.

example.en: You have no idea how much it rained!

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes the intensifying lo que, “how much”
cards.noteEn: Together with lo before a verb, que can help emphasize how much an action happens or how strong its effect is. This is different from lo que meaning “what” or “the thing that.”

example.en: You have no idea how much it rained!

cards.answerEn: to me; marks the person who feels the pain
cards.noteEn: Doler is organized differently from English “hurt”: the painful thing controls the verb, while me, te, or le identifies who feels it.

example.en: My back hurts.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish say who feels a pain?
cards.answerEn: Put me, te, le, nos, os, or les before a form of doler to identify the person who feels it.
cards.noteEn: The thing that hurts controls singular duele or plural duelen. In a completed construction, use ha or han followed by dolido; the short pronoun still names the person who feels the pain.

example.es: A Marta le duelen los pies.
example.en: Marta's feet hurt.

cards.answerEn: hurt; ached (the completed-action form used after ha)
Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

example.en: I am going to study.

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)
it (in the fixed apology lo siento, I'm sorry)

cards.noteEn: Use this fixed expression for an apology or when reacting sympathetically to bad news. Learn it as a complete expression instead of translating lo and siento separately.
cards.questionEn: What is the standard way to say “I'm sorry” when apologizing or expressing sympathy?

example.en: I'm sorry. It was a mistake.

cards.answerEn: I feel (in lo siento: I'm sorry)

cards.noteEn: Quería is a past-background form of querer. Before another action verb, it can describe an intended action that may not have happened.

example.en: I wanted to call you yesterday.

cards.questionEn: How do you tell someone that you love or care deeply for them?
cards.noteEn: Te identifies the person receiving the affection, and quiero comes from querer. The phrase is common with partners, relatives, and close friends; te amo can sound stronger or more solemn in many places.

example.en: I love you, Mom.

cards.answerEn: I love; I care deeply for (a person)
cards.noteEn: Querer usually means “to want,” but when its object is a person it commonly expresses affection or love. Te quiero is often less intense than te amo, though usage varies.

example.en: I love you very much, Grandma.

cards.promptEs: ancho fijo · texto monoespaciado · líneas alineadas
cards.answerEn: fixed-width text gives every character the same horizontal width
cards.noteEn: In a monospaced or fixed-width font, narrow letters and wide letters occupy equal space. Text strings with the same number of characters therefore have the same visual length, which is useful for code, terminals, and aligned text art.

cards.answerEn: they were (in a state or condition)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that two people or things are synchronized or in sync?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by en sincronía.
cards.noteEn: The form of estar changes for the subject and time, while en sincronía stays fixed. The expression can describe timing, movement, plans, or ideas that match.

example.es: Los dos relojes están en sincronía.
example.en: The two clocks are in sync.

cards.noteEn: Habría followed by a completed-action form such as roto describes a past result that did not actually happen or was only imagined.

example.es: Sin el mapa, me habría perdido.
example.en: Without the map, I would have gotten lost.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something would have happened in the past but did not or was only imagined?
cards.answerEn: Use a conditional form of haber such as habría, followed by the action's completed form.
cards.noteEn: The first word changes for the person: habría, habrías, habríamos, and so on. The second word stays in its completed-action form, usually ending in -ado or -ido, such as hablado or vivido; some are irregular, such as roto.

example.en: I would have accepted the offer.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks desconectarse, “to disconnect or log off”
cards.noteEn: Desconectarse uses se when the person or device leaves a connection. The form changes with the person: me desconecto, te desconectas, se desconecta.

example.es: Ana se desconectó de la llamada.
example.en: Ana disconnected from the call.
